https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c780.text: Image source, Reuters By Tabby Wilson Published 1 hour ago Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country. It follows a search of his offices over the weekend by Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators, who said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office. In his resignation letter, Kravchenko said he did not want his position to be used as a "tool for political confrontation", and referenced an earlier post in which he rejected the claims as "unsubstantiated". Corruption scandals have plagued Kyiv throughout the war against Russia, with accusations levelled at several members of President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle. According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets". The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu. Kravchenko released a statement on Sunday evening dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated", and denied any wrongdoing. He tendered his resignation a day later, thanking Zelensky and the Ukrainian parliament for their "trust". The Ukrainian president is yet to comment publicly on the resignation. Despite the creation of two Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies, Nabu and Sap, over a decade ago, corruption continues to be a significant problem in the country. In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap. Kyiv's European partners expressed alarm at the announcement, with ambassadors from the G7 group of nations warning it could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union. Ukraine is an EU candidate country, a status it was granted on condition it mounted a credible fight against corruption. Zelensky reinstated the freedom of the two anti-corruption bodies as a result of the backlash, but questions have persisted over his commitment to anti-corruption reform. Last month, Nabu said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (Â£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering . A senior official in Zelensky's office alleged to be involved was sacked. Figure caption, Fedorov asked about Ukraine government corruption claims In an interview with the BBC last month, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the president needed to be asked about his awareness of potential corruption among his closest team. "Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions," he said. During his time in office, the 35-year-old was credited with heading a drive against corruption. Since his dismissal in mid-July, after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces, he has been outspoken against what he has called a "systemic crisis of governance" in Ukraine. However, he has emphasised that he has no evidence that Zelensky is personally involved in corruption. "In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity," Federov told the BBC. https://www.politico.eu/article/in-europ.text: Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO. Cast your mind back to last year, when European leaders scrambled back and forth across the Atlantic, seeking to patch up tattered relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. After the Oval Office brawl where a scolded Zelenskyy pushed back against Trump and his vice president before being ejected from the White House, then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer and French President Emmanuel Macron led the effort to engineer a call between the pair, during which the Ukrainian president expressed regret about the meeting — but fell short of apologizing. Advertisement Advertisement Likewise, after Trump’s August summit in Alaska with Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Starmer and his top security adviser Jonathan Powell worked feverishly alongside other European leaders to rescue the broken relationship between Kyiv and Washington . They even came up with a ceasefire plan and got U.S. buy-in. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte also did some heavy lifting. But this time, after Trump unveiled a controversial diesel deal with Russia and called — once again — for Zelenskyy to step down , the European reaction has been less febrile. Of course, they have offered Kyiv strong rhetorical support and unveiled more Russia sanctions, but there has been no frantic, panicky outreach effort to Trump to mediate a speedy repair. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy looks on during a bilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, on September 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Why not? Because the Trump shock factor is wearing off, hazards Ukraine’s former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba. “The primary answer is that they have got used to him,” he told POLITICO. “They have all had an immunity shot, and they don’t feel as scared as they did last year.” “Another reason is they’re drowning in their own problems,” he added. “And I think that first they feel they have to try to figure out how what Trump is doing will impact them — how big their bill will become as a result.” European leaders are not scrambling like they did last year because Trump is “losing his leverage,” said Lia Quartapelle, an Italian lawmaker from the opposition Democratic Party who is vice chair of the parliament’s Foreign and European Affairs Committee. “We realize he cannot be trusted and we are on our own,” so there’s little point lobbying him. Advertisement Advertisement According to the Financial Times, EU officials plan to urge Zelenskyy to tone down his increasingly sharp remarks about Trump, fearing they are only inflaming the situation. Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, is positioning himself as someone who can “lay the ground” for a reconciliation, he explained to the House of Commons Wednesday. Nonetheless, the calmer reaction to Trump’s maneuvers stands out, acknowledges Daniel Fried, a former senior U.S. diplomat who served as assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian Affairs under U.S. President George W. Bush. “The Europeans seem to have taken Trump’s measure,” Fried told POLITICO. “They want to avoid the worst. They want to mitigate the damage over the next two years while Trump is in office. They do work with people in the Trump administration with whom they can work. And there are such people.” Speaking from Warsaw, fresh from attending a recent security conference in the Polish capital, he said the Europeans understand now that much of what Trump does is performative and has a short life span — like the Russian diesel deal, which has a shelf life of two or three days, he said. “I’m not sure it’s going anywhere as it is utterly impractical and legally questionable, and it isn’t clear the Russians actually can supply the diesel,” he said. In other words, why get worked up about it? Daniel Fried, Atlantic Council speaks at The 2017 Concordia Annual Summit at Grand Hyatt New York on September 19, 2017 in New York City. | Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Concordia Summit Fried said in his conversations with European leaders and officials, he has detected increasing exasperation with the overall inconsistency of the American position: “Trump wants Europe to do more militarily, but it must buy American,” he said. “But we can’t sell to the Europeans because of our needs, so they will have to wait even though they can’t build it themselves. Nonetheless, they have to carry the load in Ukraine without us. That’s utterly inconsistent, and they are exasperated by it.” And they’re just tired of having Trump jerk them around, Fried added. “One thing they are trying to avoid is having Trump snap his fingers and they come flying. Because then it looks like they are at Trump’s beck and call and are his supplicants, and they don’t want to do that. Besides, if they fly out and talk him into something, how long will what he agreed to last?” Of course, the Europeans can also console themselves with the high chance of Trump reversing himself. “There is a pattern,” said Kuleba. “He launches a cavalry attack … and then retreats. That’s what we saw in February last year. That’s what we saw in November 2025. And that’s what we will see this time too.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://aa.com.tr/en/features/explainer-.text: Americas Features EXPLAINER - What will world’s largest space congress talk about? More than 10,000 delegates, heads of major space agencies expected in Antalya on Oct. 5-9 for 77th International Astronautical Congress, 1st ever held in Türkiye Beril Canakci 04 October 2026 • Update : 04 October 2026 ISTANBUL Meeting comes weeks after US acknowledged having weapons in orbit, as tech giants race to move AI computing into space Once a year, the world’s space community gathers to debate where humanity goes next beyond Earth. This year, the list is long: weapons in orbit, artificial intelligence data centers in space, overcrowded skies and a new race to the moon. Those issues top the agenda of the 77th International Astronautical Congress, or IAC, widely described as the largest international gathering of the space sector. It will be held Oct. 5-9 at the NEST Convention Center in Belek, near the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya. It is the first time the congress has come to Türkiye since it began in 1950. Organizers expect more than 10,000 registered participants, from space agency chiefs and company executives to engineers, scientists and students. This year’s theme is “The World Needs More Space.” Here is a look at what will be discussed, who is coming and why the meeting matters. What is IAC? The congress is organized every year by the International Astronautical Federation, a nonprofit founded in 1951 to connect space organizations across national borders. The first such congress was held in Paris a year earlier, when spaceflight was still largely a dream. Today, the IAC works as a mix of scientific conference, trade fair and diplomatic summit. Researchers present thousands of technical papers, companies show off rockets and satellites in a large exhibition hall, and leaders of rival space powers share the same stage. The event has also served as a launch pad for big announcements. At the 2016 congress in Guadalajara, Mexico, SpaceX founder Elon Musk first laid out his plan to build a giant rocket to carry people to Mars, the design that later became the company’s Starship. A year later, in Adelaide, Australia used the congress to announce it would create its own national space agency. The host country changes every year, usually rotating among different continents. Last year’s congress was held in Sydney, Australia. What’s on agenda The official program covers a wide range, from moon exploration to space medicine. One headline session is titled “Geopolitics vs. Innovation,” another looks at how regional organizations govern space, and a third tackles what organizers call “orbital oversaturation.” The European Space Agency said it expects space security, exploration and the ethics of activities beyond Earth to be among the week’s themes. NASA plans to present results from its Artemis II mission and hold a news conference on the Artemis Accords, a set of US-led principles for peaceful exploration. Its Jet Propulsion Laboratory will also present its work on “trusted AI on Mars,” with a session examining how an autonomous planning system has been used to operate the Perseverance rover and how such technology could support future missions searching for life beyond Earth. The harder questions sit just outside the program’s titles. On Sept. 14, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the US Space Force already has weapons in orbit designed for “space control,” without saying what they are. It was a rare public admission that a country has operational weapons in space. Washington is also building Golden Dome, a missile shield backed by President Donald Trump that would include interceptors stationed in orbit. Officials say it could be operational by the summer of 2028, and the White House first estimated its cost at $175 billion. Critics say orbiting interceptors could double as satellite killers and push rivals to build more anti-satellite weapons of their own. Russia and China have both tested anti-satellite weapons. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the founding law of space, bans nuclear weapons in orbit but says little about conventional arms. Artificial intelligence is the other new pressure. In January, SpaceX asked US regulators for permission to launch up to 1 million satellites that would work as data centers in orbit. Google is sending its own AI chips into space for testing this week under a project called Suncatcher. Supporters say orbit offers steady solar power for energy-hungry AI. Skeptics point to high costs, radiation damage and the risk of adding still more hardware to increasingly crowded orbits, where debris from a single collision can threaten other satellites. A separate lecture at the congress will look at the safety of giant satellite networks from the viewpoint of Starlink, SpaceX’s internet constellation. Michael Nicolls, SpaceX’s senior vice president of Starlink engineering and president of SpaceXAI, will discuss the safety and sustainability challenges involved in operating a constellation on that scale. Who is coming The Global Space Leaders Summit on Oct. 6 will bring together heads and senior officials from space agencies and offices from more than 40 countries. NASA’s delegation will be led by Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson. European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher will also attend, along with India’s ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan, China’s CNSA Chief Engineer Li Guoping, JAXA President Hiroshi Yamakawa and Canadian Space Agency Acting President Jean-Claude Piedboeuf. The summit will also bring together space officials from countries including the United Arab Emirates, Brazil, Spain, the UK, France, Germany, South Korea, Pakistan, South Africa and Poland. Aarti Holla-Maini, director of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, is also set to attend the congress. The congress will also feature more than 25 astronauts, along with ministers and aerospace executives. Jonathan Cirtain, CEO and president of Axiom Space, and Mike Gold, president of Redwire, are among the industry executives attending. Other prominent industry figures include Awais Ahmed, founder and CEO of Indian space company Pixxel, and Murat Ikinci, CEO of Turkish defense and aerospace company Roketsan. The event is coordinated by Türkiye’s Ministry of Industry and Technology, hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and co-hosted by SAHA Istanbul, a defense and aerospace industry cluster, with Anadolu as its global communications partner. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription contact_the_ombudsman is_there_an_error_in_this_story LATEST NEWS All Americans increasingly dissatisfied with Trump as midterms approach: Poll Vance acknowledges ‘failures’ in US handling of Iran war Egyptian parliament adjourns session on potential military support for Saudi Arabia California wildfire forces thousands to evacuate, burns 570 acres Belgium’s consul general in Jerusalem calls Israeli occupier attack on diplomats ‘new escalation’ Zelenskyy warns US siding with Russia would be ‘historic mistake’ Turkish president congratulates Azerbaijan on Restoration of Independence Day See All US Coast Guard continues search for 6 after finding debris from missing aircraft Brazil launches probe into possible US interference amid general election

Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters View image in fullscreen ASD director general Abigail Bradshaw says ‘we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment’. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters AI (artificial intelligence) Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warns Australian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’ Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Butler Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australians should prepare for more basic and important online services to go offline unexpectedly, the nation’s signals intelligence agency has warned, urging that “system security must be prioritised over system availability”. The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) also says businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarm that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever. In its annual cyber threat report, ASD warns hostile foreign governments, criminals and hackers are using AI to gather intelligence, disrupt critical infrastructure and steal money, and that Australians should fight fire with fire. Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staff Read more “We need AI tools to help automate our defences to stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers,” the ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, said on Monday. “Australia must accelerate the modernisation of its technology and cybersecurity foundations to protect the systems we rely on every day.” The annual threat report, released on Tuesday, revealed that ASD had responded to 1,500 cybersecurity incidents in the 2025-26 year, an increase of 20% from the previous year. It also notified external entities – including businesses, governments and critical infrastructure – of more than 4,400 potential malicious cyber incidents, up 80% in a year. AI is expected to accelerate those dangers in future. ASD said government and private networks in Australia experienced “persistent” breach attempts from state-based actors last year, and claimed such actors “in the Indo-Pacific” could be launching attacks to prepare for potential future conflicts – including “future intelligence collection or disruption activities”. The agency said the increasing availability of AI was creating positive opportunities, but also allowing cybercriminals and state-based actors to find vulnerabilities and launch attacks faster and more effectively. ASD warned “all network owners are facing elevated threat levels”, saying cybersecurity was now a “core business risk and leadership responsibility” for all organisations, no longer only a technical concern. The report said integrating AI tools into cybersecurity functions could help find potential weaknesses or suspicious behaviour, and improve responses. “To strengthen our cyber defences, we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment,” Bradshaw said. She has spoken previously about ASD having access to Anthropic’s Mythos model , the powerful AI tool which the frontier lab said it couldn’t release publicly because it could identify unknown flaws in IT systems. While the use of AI by malicious actors is on the rise, Australian government agencies believe having access to such frontier models and collaborating with leading AI labs is critical to bolstering cybersecurity. “To stay ahead, Australians must enhance their cyber defences while harnessing AI’s benefit,” the defence minister, Richard Marles, said on the report’s release. Tony Burke, the minister for home affairs and cybersecurity, said the government was “positioning Australia to respond to the evolving threats and opportunities presented by emerging technologies”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Bradshaw said “legacy technology”, such as outdated systems or devices that were no longer supported with new updates by their creators, were among the biggest risks and most attractive targets for hackers. ASD called for Australia to modernise technology and cybersecurity capabilities, and said all organisations must take stronger action to ward off new threats. Last week, newly discovered vulnerabilities in PHP – a programming language that underpins most websites – triggered a rush by governments and businesses to fix the problem. The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on | Peter Lewis Read more ASD urged organisations to update their systems, seek help from ASD and report suspicious incidents. Bradshaw and Marles said organisations should prioritise the security of their systems over keeping them online, which could mean more services are forced to go offline while they are secured. “In a threat environment transformed by AI, collective action is our strongest defence,” Bradshaw said. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: Jared Kushner, lead negotiator for the US, with the UAE’s foreign minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan at the talks on Tuesday Photograph: Rula Rouhana/Reuters View image in fullscreen Jared Kushner, lead negotiator for the US, with the UAE’s foreign minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan at the talks on Tuesday Photograph: Rula Rouhana/Reuters Ukraine US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe Europe live – latest updates Andrew Roth in Washington and Jennifer Rankin Tue 10 Nov 2026 07.48 EST First published on Tue 10 Nov 2026 00.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine , beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February. The talks are the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home. The first day of talks ended early Tuesday afternoon local time with a second day set for Wednesday. Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe , administration officials have said. European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west. View image in fullscreen Participants at the trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Photograph: Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service Press Office/AP Before the trilateral talks, European officials held separate discussions on Tuesday with representatives from Ukraine and the US, where they agreed “any future arrangements must respect sovereignty, territorial integrity, independent decision-making, and provide credible security guarantees for Ukraine”, according to a joint statement. European leaders are not convinced Russia intends to negotiate in good faith. “So far they have just been pretending that they negotiate because we haven’t seen any ⁠goodwill from the Russian side,” the EU high representative for foreign policy, Kaja Kallas, told Reuters on Monday. European countries want to be involved in discussions, although there are signs of unease about the proliferating strands of peace talks. Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, last week complained about the “disorderly” process of meetings and phone calls that she argued weakened Europe’s ability to speak with one voice. Since his first decade in power, Vladimir Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal. View image in fullscreen Members of the Ukrainian delegation, led by Rustem Umerov, at the talks. Photograph: Grigory Sysoyev/Reuters Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal. The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protects member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine. “What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said. “Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.” Critics have expressed scepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response. View image in fullscreen The Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky at the talks. Photograph: Rula Rouhana/Reuters Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the US, described a potential new framework for Europe in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”. European delegations from Germany, France, the UK, Italy and the EU will meet US negotiators in Abu Dhabi to discuss the “long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe in order to figure out how to reduce future conflicts”. A European security official from a country attending the talks said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations. “We already have a European security architecture in place,” said Kallas at a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday. “This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.” Donald Trump has also said that Ukraine would probably be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape”. View image in fullscreen Trump and Zelenskyy in Florida in December 2025. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP After meeting the Kremlin adviser Kirill Dmitriev last week, Trump said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia. “There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe. At that time, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal, and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later. The US administration official said: “We have to build something new that works today … Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war.” The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”. “We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.
